docs.title: I Have a Question
docs.text:
If you want to ask a question, we assume that you have read the available Documentation.

Before you ask a question, it is best to search for existing Issues that might help you. In case you have found a suitable issue and still need clarification, you can write your question in this issue. It is also advisable to search the internet for answers first.

If you then still feel the need to ask a question and need clarification, we recommend the following:

  • Open an Issue.
  • Provide as much context as you can about what you're running into.
  • Provide your OS, Python version, conda version, kmhelpers version, and kmindex version, depending on what seems relevant.

We will then take care of the issue as soon as possible.

docs.title: Legal Notice
docs.text: When contributing to this project, you must agree that you have authored 100% of the content, that you have the necessary rights to the content and that the content you contribute may be provided under the project license (GPL-3.0-only).

docs.title: Before Submitting a Bug Report
docs.text:
A good bug report shouldn't leave others needing to chase you up for more information. Therefore, we ask you to investigate carefully, collect information and describe the issue in detail in your report. Please complete the following steps in advance to help us fix any potential bug as fast as possible.

  • Make sure that you are using the latest version.
  • Determine if your bug is really a bug and not an error on your side e.g. using an incompatible environment or version of kmindex (Make sure that you have read the documentation. If you are looking for support, you might want to check this section).
  • Also make sure to search the internet (including Stack Overflow) to see if users outside of the GitHub community have discussed the issue.
  • Collect information about the bug:
  • Stack trace (Traceback)
  • OS, platform and version (Linux x86_64, macOS Intel, macOS Apple Silicon)
  • Python version and conda environment details (conda info, pip show pykmhelpers)
  • kmhelpers version (kh --version)
  • Version of kmindex, kmtricks, and ntCard (kmindex --version, kmtricks --version, ntcard --version)
  • Possibly your input (JSONL sample list, YAML config) and the output
  • If kmhelpers crashed, attach the dump file (kmhelpers_<timestamp>.dump) written to your working directory
  • Can you reliably reproduce the issue? And can you also reproduce it with older versions?

docs.title: How Do I Submit a Good Bug Report?
docs.text:
You must never report security related issues, vulnerabilities or bugs including sensitive information to the issue tracker, or elsewhere in public. Instead sensitive bugs must be sent by email to kmhelpers@groupes.renater.fr.

We use GitHub issues to track bugs and errors. If you run into an issue with the project:

  • Open an Issue. (Since we can't be sure at this point whether it is a bug or not, we ask you not to talk about a bug yet and not to label the issue.)
  • Explain the behavior you would expect and the actual behavior.
  • Please provide as much context as possible and describe the reproduction steps that someone else can follow to recreate the issue on their own. This usually includes the command you ran and the relevant input files or configuration. For good bug reports you should isolate the problem and create a reduced test case.
  • Provide the information you collected in the previous section.

Once it's filed:

  • The project team will label the issue accordingly.
  • A team member will try to reproduce the issue with your provided steps. If there are no reproduction steps or no obvious way to reproduce the issue, the team will ask you for those steps and mark the issue as needs-repro. Bugs with the needs-repro tag will not be addressed until they are reproduced.
  • If the team is able to reproduce the issue, it will be marked needs-fix, as well as possibly other tags (such as critical), and the issue will be left to be implemented by someone.

docs.title: Suggesting Enhancements
docs.text: This section guides you through submitting an enhancement suggestion for kmhelpers, including completely new features and minor improvements to existing functionality. Following these guidelines will help maintainers and the community to understand your suggestion and find related suggestions.

docs.title: Before Submitting an Enhancement
docs.text:
• Make sure that you are using the latest version.
  • Read the documentation carefully and find out if the functionality is already covered, maybe by an individual configuration.
  • Perform a search to see if the enhancement has already been suggested. If it has, add a comment to the existing issue instead of opening a new one.
  • Find out whether your idea fits with the scope and aims of the project. It's up to you to make a strong case to convince the project's developers of the merits of this feature. Keep in mind that we want features that will be useful to the majority of our users and not just a small subset.

docs.title: How Do I Submit a Good Enhancement Suggestion?
docs.text:
Enhancement suggestions are tracked as GitHub issues.

  • Use a clear and descriptive title for the issue to identify the suggestion.
  • Provide a step-by-step description of the suggested enhancement in as many details as possible.
  • Describe the current behavior and explain which behavior you expected to see instead and why. At this point you can also tell which alternatives do not work for you.
  • Explain why this enhancement would be useful to most kmhelpers users. You may also want to point out other projects that solved it better and which could serve as inspiration.

docs.title: Setting up the development environment
docs.text:
1. Fork and clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/kmhelpers
cd kmhelpers

  2. Create the conda environment and install kmhelpers in editable mode: 

    conda env create -f conda/environment.yml -p ./.env
conda activate ./.env
pip install -e ".[dev]"

  3. Run the test suite to verify everything is working: 

    pytest

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
• Create a feature branch from main: git checkout -b feature/my-feature
  • Make your changes and add tests under pykmhelpers/tests/
  • Ensure all checks pass before opening a pull request: 
    black pykmhelpers          # format
flake8 pykmhelpers         # lint
mypy pykmhelpers           # type-check
pytest                     # tests
  • Open a pull request against the main branch.

docs.title: Improving The Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs Material and hosted at https://sebllns.github.io/kmhelpers/.

To preview the docs locally:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve

Source files live under docs/. Please keep the documentation consistent with any code changes you make.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
• Formatter: Black with line-length = 88. Run black pykmhelpers before committing.
  • Linter: Flake8. Run flake8 pykmhelpers before committing.
  • Type hints: encouraged. Run mypy pykmhelpers to check.
  • Import order: isort with the black profile.

docs.title: Commit Messages
docs.text:
• Use the imperative mood: "Add feature", not "Added feature".
  • Keep the subject line under 72 characters.
  • Reference related issues where applicable: Fix #42 — ….
  • Notable changes should be reflected in CHANGELOG.md under the relevant version section.

docs.title: Join The Project Team
docs.text: If you are interested in becoming a regular contributor or maintainer, reach out by opening an issue or contacting us at kmhelpers@groupes.renater.fr.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
This guide is based on the contributing-gen. Make your own!

PPenloglou-WMF, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: Dev environment setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/sebllns/kmhelpers
cd kmhelpers
pip install -e ".[dev]"

kmindex and kmtricks must also be available, see Installation.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
pykmhelpers/
  cli/          # Click commands (one file per command)
  core/         # Low-level building blocks (index, bloom_filter, kmindex_wrapper, ...)
  operations/   # Higher-level operations (builder, fof_validation, ...)
  tests/        # Test suite
  pipeline/     # Pipeline execution engine

Each CLI command in cli/ is a thin layer that delegates to operations/ or core/.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
pytest

Coverage is reported automatically (configured in pyproject.toml). HTML report is written to htmlcov/.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
Tool Purpose black Formatting (line length 88) flake8 Linting mypy Type checking 
black pykmhelpers/
flake8 pykmhelpers/
mypy pykmhelpers/

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Branch Purpose Updated by main Development trunk, always passing CI; releases are tags vX.Y.Z on it PR feature/<name>, fix/<name>, doc/<name>, ci/<name>, release/vX.Y.Z Short-lived work, deleted after merge Direct push docs Hidden docs preview, for docs work in progress Direct push paper JOSS paper; paper.pdf is committed by CI Direct push gh-pages Generated by the docs workflow, never edited by hand CI

main is protected: changes land through pull requests. Users install from tags, PyPI or bioconda, not from main.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
git checkout main
git pull
git checkout -b feature/my-feature
# ... commit ...
git push -u origin feature/my-feature
gh pr create --base main
# after review and green CI:
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch    # or --merge to keep each commit

Rules:

  • One branch per topic, from an up-to-date main, deleted after merge.
  • To bring new main commits into a pushed branch, use git merge main; rebase only before the first push.
  • git push --force-with-lease only on your own, unshared branch.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Docs are versioned with mike on the gh-pages branch, deployed by .github/workflows/docs.yml:

Trigger Deployed as URL Push to docs Hidden preview /kmhelpers/preview/ Push to main Version main, titled main (<short hash>), overwritten each time /kmhelpers/main/ Tag vX.Y.Z Version X.Y.Z, alias latest (default) /kmhelpers/X.Y.Z/

Content specific to a release or to the development version goes between release-only or dev-only HTML comment markers; @VERSION@ inside a release block is replaced by the version (see scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py, used in docs/getting-started/installation.md). Release builds get DOCS_RELEASE=X.Y.Z from the workflow; to preview one locally:

DOCS_RELEASE=X.Y.Z mkdocs serve

To try docs changes before merging, push them to docs (git push --force origin HEAD:docs) and open the preview.

Manual deploy from any branch or tag (the branch must be pushed):

# Redeploy a release from its tag
gh workflow run docs.yml --ref vX.Y.Z

# Deploy a branch as a given version, without moving "latest"
gh workflow run docs.yml --ref fix/docs-typo -f version=X.Y.Z -f latest=false

# Deploy and remove an old version
gh workflow run docs.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f delete_version=<old>

# Follow the run
gh run watch $(gh run list --workflow docs.yml --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')

Without -f version, the version is the package version of the ref (main on main). latest defaults to true. A release version gets the release-only blocks, like a tag build.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: pykmhelpers/_version.py is the single source of the version. Commands below use VERSION=X.Y.Z.

docs.title: 1. Prepare
docs.text:
git checkout main
git pull
git checkout -b release/v$VERSION
  • Set __version__ = "X.Y.Z" in pykmhelpers/_version.py.
  • Add the ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD section to CHANGELOG.md. It becomes the GitHub release notes, so it must be written before tagging.
pytest
rm -rf dist && python -m build && twine check dist/*
git commit -am "release: v$VERSION"
git push -u origin release/v$VERSION

docs.title: 2. Merge into main
docs.text:
gh pr create --base main --title "Release v$VERSION" --body "See CHANGELOG.md"
gh pr checks --watch
gh pr merge --merge --delete-branch

docs.title: 3. Tag
docs.text:
git checkout main
git pull
git tag -a v$VERSION -m "kmhelpers v$VERSION" \
    -m "Documentation: https://sebllns.github.io/kmhelpers/$VERSION/
Changelog: https://sebllns.github.io/kmhelpers/$VERSION/changelog/"
git push origin v$VERSION

Or with git create-release (scripts/git-create-release, requires gh), which runs the commands above after checks, then lists the release workflow runs:

git create-release [--view] [--overwrite] [VERSION]

VERSION defaults to pykmhelpers/_version.py; a different one asks for confirmation. Before tagging, it checks that CHANGELOG.md has the ## [VERSION] section, that the tag does not exist, that the working tree is clean and that HEAD is origin/main.

Option Effect --view Show the release and the workflow runs, no tagging --overwrite Delete the GitHub release and the tag, then tag again -h Help (--help is caught by git for aliases)

The alias is defined in the versioned .gitconfig, enable it once per clone:

git config include.path ../.gitconfig

Never move or re-create a pushed tag, except with --overwrite when the release failed before the PyPI upload.

docs.title: 4. Automatic steps
docs.text:
Pushing the tag runs:

  • release.yml: builds the sdist and wheel, creates the GitHub release with the files attached and notes made of .github/release-notes.md (docs links, install and update commands), the CHANGELOG section and the merged PRs, then uploads the files to PyPI (publish job) and installs the published version in a fresh environment to check kmhelpers --version (verify job).
  • docs.yml: deploys the docs as version X.Y.Z with alias latest.
gh run list --limit 4
gh release view v$VERSION    # or: git create-release --view

docs.title: 5. Approve the PyPI upload (browser)
docs.text:
The publish job runs in the pypi environment, which waits for a manual approval:

  1. Open the "Release build" run of the tag in the Actions tab.
  2. Once tests and build are green, check the release: notes, sdist and wheel attached.
  3. Click "Review deployments", select pypi, then "Approve and deploy".
  4. When publish and verify are green, check the version on PyPI and the docs at https://sebllns.github.io/kmhelpers/X.Y.Z/.

A PyPI version cannot be uploaded twice: a broken release is fixed by a new version.

docs.title: 6. Bioconda
docs.text: After the PyPI upload, the bioconda bot opens a PR in bioconda-recipes updating the version and sha256. Check that runtime dependencies still match pyproject.toml, then approve it.

docs.title: Patch of an older version
docs.text:
Only when a fix must be released for a version older than main. The tag is created manually, as git create-release only tags origin/main:

git checkout -b maint/vX.Y v$OLD_VERSION
# commit the fix, bump the version, add the CHANGELOG section
git push -u origin maint/vX.Y
git tag -a v$PATCH_VERSION -m "kmhelpers v$PATCH_VERSION"
git push origin v$PATCH_VERSION

Then bring the fix and the CHANGELOG section into main through a PR. This tag gets the latest docs alias; redeploy the newest release afterwards with gh workflow run docs.yml --ref v<newest>.

docs.title: Building the Documentation
docs.text: The docs are built with MkDocs using the Material theme.

docs.title: Install dependencies
docs.text:
For development:

pip install -e ".[dev]"

For docs only:

pip install -e ".[docs]"

docs.title: Live preview
docs.text:
Starts a local server with hot-reload on file changes:

mkdocs serve --dirtyreload --livereload

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser.

docs.title: Build static site
docs.text:
Outputs the static HTML to site/:

mkdocs build

The site/ directory is git-ignored and should not be committed.

docs.title: Adding or editing pages
docs.text:
1. Edit or create a .md file under docs/.
  2. If it's a new page, add it to the nav: section in mkdocs.yml.
  3. Run mkdocs serve to preview.

docs.title: Deploying to GitHub Pages
docs.text: Docs are versioned with mike. Do not use mkdocs gh-deploy - it overwrites the entire gh-pages branch and destroys version history.

docs.title: Deploy a new version
docs.text:
mike deploy --push --update-aliases <version> latest

Example for a release:

mike deploy --push --update-aliases 0.8.0 latest

This builds the docs, pushes them to gh-pages under /<version>/, and updates the latest alias to point to it.

docs.title: List deployed versions
docs.text: mike list

docs.title: Preview versioned docs locally
docs.text: mike serve

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
New to kmhelpers?

Start here: install the toolkit, then walk through the pipeline with a quick, hands-on example.

  1. Installation: set up kmhelpers and its dependencies (kmindex, kmtricks, ntCard) via Conda
  2. Quick Start: learn the design → build → query pipeline and common use cases
  3. Tutorial: Once you're set up, walk through a full, real-data example end to end.

By Glosome - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Once kmhelpers is installed, the fastest way to get hands-on is the E. coli tutorial - it builds a queryable index from real data in three commands. For syntax and options on any command, see the Command Reference.

Tip

kh is available as a short alias for kmhelpers - both commands are identical.

docs.title: The Pipeline
docs.text:
kmhelpers exposes the index lifecycle as a sequence of commands, illustrated in figure below:

Command breakdown
  • list - recursively discovers all samples in a given directory and counts each sample's distinct \(k\)-mers using ntcard (unless the counts are provided by the user).
  • profile - determines the best set of sub-index BF sizes given the user-defined maximum number of sub-indexes and target false-positive rate.
  • compose - assigns each sample to its sub-index and generates the files-of-files describing the data origin of each sub-index.
  • plan - validates sample files, available disk space, and memory upfront, and emits ready-to-execute pipeline scripts.
  • apply - builds all sub-indexes by invoking kmindex, with span-level and name-level filtering.

For ease of use, steps list, profile, and compose can be grouped under a single command named design, and steps plan and apply can be grouped under the build command.

Once an index is built, kmhelpers also answers queries (query). Multi-step workflows can be described as declarative YAML pipelines (pipeline) and executed in a single command.

An additional command, manage (under development), lets users register several distinct indexes (built locally or hosted anywhere accessible) into one logical index, redirecting each query to all registered indexes at query time.

Indices are built and queried in three steps:

[1] design → [2] build → [3] query
Step Command Purpose Input Output 1 design Discover samples and generate index definitions directory or sample list index definitions 2 build Build k-mer indices from those definitions index definitions built k-mer index 3 query Search the indices with FASTA/FASTQ sequences built index + query sequences match results

docs.title: Create a new index
docs.text:
Turn a collection of samples into a searchable index, from nothing. Input: your sequence files. Output: a queryable index.

Run the pipeline steps against a directory of sequence files (or a plain-text / YAML sample list):

Commands 
kmhelpers design /data/sequences -o coli_db/ -n coli
kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/*/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

Your index is ready to query:

Commands 
kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ query.fa

See the E. coli tutorial for a full walkthrough.

docs.title: Update an existing index
docs.text:
Add new samples to an index you already built, without starting over. Input: an existing index, plus the new samples to add. Output: the same index, now also containing the new samples.

Re-run design with the same -o/-n and a new sample source, tagging the run with a fresh -S session ID:

Commands 
kmhelpers design coli_5_update.txt -o coli_db/ -n coli -S update
kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/update/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

design detects the existing layout file at coli_db/compose/coli_layout.yaml, skips the profile step, and composes only the new samples. build then merges the new samples into the existing index automatically, without recounting the samples already indexed.

Disk space

kmindex cannot add samples to an existing index in place, so the update merges the previous samples and the new ones into a complete new index, which replaces the previous one in its folder (coli_build/coli_g0/). Both versions coexist on disk during the merge, so plan for at least twice the size of the sub-indices being updated.

The previous version is deleted once the updated one is registered and checked; --keep-previous keeps it to compare both - see build - Updating an index.

docs.title: Query sequences in an index
docs.text:
Check whether given sequences are present in your samples. Input: a built index, plus the sequences you want to search for. Output: for each sequence, which samples it was found in.

Point query at a built registry (-r) with one or more FASTA/FASTQ files, directories, or stdin:

Commands 
# Query the whole index (all sub-indices)
kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ query.fa

# Query specific sub-indices with multiple threads
kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -n coli_g0 -n coli_g1 -t 4 -o results/ query.fa

# Scan a directory of query files, or read from stdin
kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ ./queries_dir/
cat query.fa | kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ -

See query for batching, output formats, and threshold options.

docs.title: Work with large datasets: automatic vs manual build
docs.text:
Build large indices safely and faster, by checking the work before it runs and spreading it across multiple machines. Input: the same index definitions produced by design or compose. Output: the same built index, produced manually step-by-step for more flexibility.

For large sample counts, prefer running plan and apply separately instead of build (which chains them). plan validates all sample paths and writes a ready-to-run shell script to OUTPUT_DIR/assets/ up front, so path errors surface before any CPU/I/O-intensive building starts:

Commands 
kmhelpers plan coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

Automatic build

Review coli_build/assets/ and coli_build/logs/, then:

Commands 
kmhelpers apply coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

Manual build

plan also writes plain bash scripts equivalent to running apply in OUTPUT_DIR/assets/: one self-contained script per sub-index (<name>_g<span>_<session>.sh: builds, merge, cleanup), and kmhelpers_apply.sh, which runs them all in order. They can be run manually for a fully hands-on build, and since each sub-index script is independent, they are easy to dispatch for distributed computing - e.g. one job per script in a cluster job scheduler:

Commands 
kmhelpers plan coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/
bash coli_build/assets/kmhelpers_apply.sh

apply itself remains as an useful alternative, including on distributed systems - it can be launched independently on each node (e.g. one --span or --name subset per node) just like the bash script, lets you filter or rerun specific builds by name/span, and can email a notification on completion:

Commands 
# each node builds a disjoint subset, and emails when its share is done
kmhelpers apply coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/ -n coli_g0 --notify you@example.com
kmhelpers apply coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/ -n coli_g1 --notify you@example.com

git fetch --tags

docs.title: Tutorial: Indexing 10 E. coli Assemblies
docs.text: By the end you will have a queryable k-mer index of these assemblies built in three commands: design → build → query.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• kmhelpers installed (see Installation)
  • Command wget to download the dataset
  • ~200 MB of free disk space for the dataset + resulting index

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The following tools are installed alongside kmhelpers when using the conda environment:

  • kmindex - the underlying indexing engine
  • ntcard - k-mer counter used by list

docs.title: Step 1 - Download the dataset
docs.text:
mkdir -p coli_dataset && cd coli_dataset
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/780/515/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/001/076/125/GCA_001076125.1_ASM107612v1/GCA_001076125.1_ASM107612v1_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/001/417/575/GCA_001417575.1_ASM141757v1/GCA_001417575.1_ASM141757v1_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/944/435/GCA_000944435.1_Ec57A_E8C1_MIRA_assembly/GCA_000944435.1_Ec57A_E8C1_MIRA_assembly_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/001/075/925/GCA_001075925.1_ASM107592v1/GCA_001075925.1_ASM107592v1_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/936/715/GCA_000936715.1_E8C1_assembly/GCA_000936715.1_E8C1_assembly_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/939/215/GCA_000939215.1_Ec57A_A7_MIRA_assembly/GCA_000939215.1_Ec57A_A7_MIRA_assembly_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/001/413/795/GCA_001413795.1_ASM141379v1/GCA_001413795.1_ASM141379v1_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/001/373/195/GCA_001373195.1_57A_A7_assembly/GCA_001373195.1_57A_A7_assembly_genomic.fna.gz"
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/938/575/GCA_000938575.1_D1C4_assembly/GCA_000938575.1_D1C4_assembly_genomic.fna.gz"
cd ..
I/O

Input: 10 NCBI FTP URLs Output: coli_dataset/

docs.title: Step 2 - Design the index (design)
docs.text:
kmhelpers design coli_dataset/ \
    -o coli_db/ \
    -n coli \
    -S initial \
    -k 25 \
    -b 1.1 \
    -g 2
I/O

Input: coli_dataset/, scanned for sequence files (one sample per file) Output: coli_db/list/ (JSONL), coli_db/profile/ (profile.yaml, groups.png), coli_db/compose/ (index definitions)

INFO

design runs list → profile → compose in a single command. For a detailed walkthrough of each sub-command, see Step-by-step: list → profile → compose.

Why scan a directory rather than pass a sample list?

A directory scan names each sample after its file and counts its k-mers. A sample list lets you set names, reuse k-mer counts, group files freely and mix locations - see When to use a sample list.

docs.title: Step 3 - Build the index (build)
docs.text:
kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/ --show-progress
I/O

Input: coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml Output: coli_build/index.json + one folder per sub-index, coli_build/coli_g0/ and coli_build/coli_g1/ - ready-to-query index

INFO

build runs plan → apply in a single command, validating all paths before starting the build. For a detailed walkthrough, or to run plan first and apply later with bash or apply, see Step-by-step: plan → apply.

docs.title: Step 4 - Query the index (query)
docs.text:
Extract the first contig of the first sample as a query sequence:

zcat coli_dataset/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1_genomic.fna.gz \
    | awk '/^>/{n++} n==2{exit} {print}' > query.fa

Then query the index:

kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ query.fa
I/O

Input: coli_build/ (index root), query.fa (first contig of GCA_000780515) Output: results/

RESULT

query merges the results of all sub-indices into results/query/results.tsv, one row per query sequence and one column per matching sample:

seq GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1_genomic
JSPL01000060.1  1.000

Each value is the fraction of query k-mers found in that sample. Samples scoring below the threshold (-R, default 0.05) are omitted. Use -f to select another output format (json, yaml, md, html). GCA_000780515 scores 1.0 -- a perfect match, as expected since query.fa was extracted from that assembly.

docs.title: Tutorial: the Python API
docs.text:
This page runs the E. coli tutorial and its update from Python. Each CLI command wraps a class of pykmhelpers, and this page calls those classes directly:

CLI Python list SampleLister profile SpanProfiler compose IndexComposer plan / apply IndexOps with ApplyMode.PLAN / ApplyMode.APPLY query QueryRunner

design and build are chains of these classes, written below as two small functions. Parameters are the ones of the CLI tutorial, so both produce the same coli_db/ and coli_build/ trees.

The complete script is examples/tuto_ecoli_api.py:

python examples/tuto_ecoli_api.py my_workdir/

For more control over each step, see Python API (advanced).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Same as the E. coli tutorial: kmhelpers installed, with kmindex and ntcard on PATH.

The classes log through the standard logging module. Enable it to follow the progress:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s | %(message)s")

docs.title: Step 1 - Download the dataset
docs.text:
Run the wget commands of Step 1 of the CLI tutorial, or download from Python:

import os
import urllib.request

NCBI = "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA"
DATASET = [
    "000/780/515/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1",
    "001/076/125/GCA_001076125.1_ASM107612v1",
    "001/417/575/GCA_001417575.1_ASM141757v1",
    "000/944/435/GCA_000944435.1_Ec57A_E8C1_MIRA_assembly",
    "001/075/925/GCA_001075925.1_ASM107592v1",
    "000/936/715/GCA_000936715.1_E8C1_assembly",
    "000/939/215/GCA_000939215.1_Ec57A_A7_MIRA_assembly",
    "001/413/795/GCA_001413795.1_ASM141379v1",
    "001/373/195/GCA_001373195.1_57A_A7_assembly",
    "000/938/575/GCA_000938575.1_D1C4_assembly",
]


def download(accessions, out_dir):
    """Download NCBI assemblies into out_dir, skipping files already there."""
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    for acc in accessions:
        name = f"{os.path.basename(acc)}_genomic.fna.gz"
        path = os.path.join(out_dir, name)
        if not os.path.exists(path):
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{NCBI}/{acc}/{name}", path)


download(DATASET, "coli_dataset")
I/O

Input: 10 NCBI FTP URLs Output: coli_dataset/

docs.title: Step 2 - Design the index (list → profile → compose)
docs.text:
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.composer import IndexComposer
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.index_db import IndexDB
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.sample_lister import SampleLister
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.span_profiler import SpanProfiler


def reset_index_registry():
    """Free the index names held by IndexDB, a process-wide registry.

    Compose and build each create IndexDB objects named after the indexes;
    a second one with the same name in the same process raises an error.
    """
    for db in IndexDB.get_all() or []:
        if db.name:
            IndexDB.remove_instance(db.name)


def design(input_dir, session, profile=True):
    """list -> profile -> compose, the steps of `kmhelpers design`."""
    jsonl = f"coli_db/list/coli_samples_{session}.jsonl"
    os.makedirs("coli_db/list", exist_ok=True)

    # list: one sample per file, k-mers counted with ntcard
    SampleLister(
        output_file=jsonl,
        input_dir=input_dir,
        kmer_size=25,
        is_assembled=True,
        do_grouping=False,
    ).run()

    # profile: Bloom filter spans, split into 2 groups (initial session only)
    if profile:
        SpanProfiler(
            input_file=jsonl,
            output_dir="coli_db/profile",
            n_groups=2,
            base=1.1,
        ).run()

    # compose: a new index from the profile, or an update from the layout
    reset_index_registry()
    IndexComposer(
        profiles_file="coli_db/profile/profile.yaml" if profile else None,
        layout_file=None if profile else "coli_db/compose/coli_layout.yaml",
        name="coli",
    ).run(input_file=jsonl, output_dir="coli_db/compose", run_id=session)
    return f"coli_db/compose/coli/{session}/coli.yaml"


definition = design("coli_dataset", "initial")

CLI equivalent: kmhelpers design coli_dataset/ -o coli_db/ -n coli -S initial -k 25 -b 1.1 -g 2

I/O

Input: coli_dataset/, scanned for sequence files (one sample per file) Output: coli_db/list/ (JSONL), coli_db/profile/ (profile.yaml, groups.png), coli_db/compose/ (index definitions, coli_layout.yaml)

INFO

IndexDB keeps every index definition in a class-level registry keyed by name. The CLI runs each command in a new process; in a single Python process, free the names with reset_index_registry() before each compose and build.

Why scan a directory rather than pass a sample list?

A directory scan names each sample after its file and counts its k-mers. A sample list lets you set names, reuse k-mer counts, group files freely and mix locations - see When to use a sample list.

API defaults

Some defaults of the classes differ from the CLI: SampleLister groups by leaf folder (do_grouping=True) and SpanProfiler uses base=2.0. Pass these parameters explicitly.

Customize SampleLister (list) Parameter CLI Effect input_dir / input_list INPUT Directory to scan, or a plain-text / YAML sample list kmer_size -k K-mer size used for counting is_assembled -dt True: distinct k-mers (assemblies); False: solid k-mers (raw reads) do_count -nc False skips ntcard do_grouping -lg One sample per leaf folder pair_regex --paired Group mate files (R1/R2) into one sample; DEFAULT_PAIR_REGEX in pykmhelpers.core.constants do_continue -c Resume from an existing output file autorename -a Rename duplicate sample IDs instead of skipping them ntcard_threads -ntt Threads used by ntcard Customize SpanProfiler (profile) Parameter CLI Effect n_groups -g Number of storage-balanced groups (sub-indexes) base -b Base of the span buckets: closer to 1 means finer buckets false_positive_rate -fp Bloom filter false-positive rate Customize IndexComposer (compose) Parameter CLI Effect profiles_file / layout_file -pf New index from a profile, or update from the existing layout selected_profile -pr Profile to use from profile.yaml (default: the one set by profile) shard_size -si Maximum size of one shard, in bytes (parse_shard_size("256GB") from pykmhelpers.cli.shared) partition_count -p Partitions per index, 0 for automatic abundance_min - Minimum k-mer abundance written to the definitions kmer_size, false_positive_rate - Override the values read from the JSONL header and profile format - Definition file format (yaml by default)

docs.title: Step 3 - Build the index (plan → apply)
docs.text:
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.index_ops import (
    ApplyMode,
    ApplyStatus,
    IndexOps,
    IndexOpsConfig,
)


def build(definition):
    """plan -> apply, the steps of `kmhelpers build`."""
    reset_index_registry()
    ops = IndexOps(IndexOpsConfig(workdir="coli_build"))

    result = ops.run(definition, mode=ApplyMode.PLAN)
    ops.write_script()  # coli_build/assets/<session>/kmhelpers_apply.sh
    assert result.status is not ApplyStatus.FAILED, "plan failed"

    result = ops.run(definition, mode=ApplyMode.APPLY, fail_on_error=True)
    assert result.status is not ApplyStatus.FAILED, "apply failed"


build(definition)

CLI equivalent: kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

I/O

Input: coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml Output: coli_build/index.json + one folder per sub-index, coli_build/coli_g0/ and coli_build/coli_g1/, build scripts in coli_build/assets/initial/

INFO

run() returns an ApplyResult: status is SUCCESS, PARTIAL (some indexes failed, only with fail_on_error=False), FAILED or NONE (nothing to do), and details holds the per-index report written to coli_build/logs/ by the CLI.

Customize IndexOpsConfig (plan, apply, build) Parameter CLI Effect kmindex_threads -t Threads per build, None to size them from the resource limits limits, safety_margin --limits, --safety-margin Resource limits (ram, files, threads) and the fraction of detected limits to use max_chunks --max-chunks Cap on the chunks one index is split into partition_count -p Override the number of partitions minimizer_length --minim-size Minimizer size kmindex_skip_compression -NC Do not compress intermediate files keep_previous --keep-previous Keep the replaced version of an updated index sample_rootpath -b Base path for relative sample paths

ApplyMode.APPLY_SHOW_PROGRESS is the --show-progress animation, and ApplyMode.DRY_RUN only generates the commands.

docs.title: Step 4 - Query the index (query)
docs.text:
Extract the first contig of GCA_000780515, then query it:

import gzip

from pykmhelpers import QueryRunner, QueryRunnerConfig


def first_contig(fasta_gz, out_file):
    """Write the first sequence of a gzipped FASTA file to out_file."""
    with gzip.open(fasta_gz, "rt") as fin, open(out_file, "w") as fout:
        for n, line in enumerate(fin):
            if line.startswith(">") and n > 0:
                break
            fout.write(line)


def query(query_file, output_dir):
    """Query the index, return {sample: best score}."""
    runner = QueryRunner(
        QueryRunnerConfig(
            registry_path="coli_build",
            output_dir=output_dir,
            output_format="tsv",
        )
    )
    scores = {}
    for result in runner.run([query_file])[0]:
        for queries in result.items.values():
            for samples in queries.values():
                for sample, score in samples.items():
                    scores[sample] = max(scores.get(sample, 0.0), score)
    return scores


first_contig("coli_dataset/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1_genomic.fna.gz", "query.fa")
print(query("query.fa", "results"))

CLI equivalent: kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results/ query.fa

I/O

Input: coli_build/, query.fa Output: results/query/ (results.tsv, statistics, raw kmindex output), and the results as Python objects

RESULT 
{'GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1_genomic': 1.0}

run() returns, per query file, one KmindexQueryResult per sub-index. Their items are {index: {query: {sample: score}}}, the scores of results/query/results.tsv. To merge and summarize them, see advanced.

Customize QueryRunnerConfig (query) Parameter CLI Effect index_ids -n Query only these sub-indexes zvalue -z Findere z: effective false-positive rate p^z threshold -R Minimum score kept threads -t kmindex threads batch, single_query -b, -s Concatenate files or sequences into one query output_format, export -f, -x Data format (tsv, json, yaml, None) and human report (md, html) on_existing, force -e Existing output directory: skip (default, returns no result), fail, delete stats --stats Write sequence_stats.tsv and sample_stats.tsv on_result - Callback called with each query's results, see advanced

docs.title: Update the index
docs.text:
As in Update an existing index: download the new sample into its own directory, design an update session against the existing layout (no profile step), and build it into the same coli_build/.

UPDATE = ["000/005/845/GCA_000005845.2_ASM584v2"]

download(UPDATE, "coli_update")
definition = design("coli_update", "update", profile=False)
build(definition)

first_contig("coli_update/GCA_000005845.2_ASM584v2_genomic.fna.gz", "query_update.fa")
print(query("query_update.fa", "results_update"))
print(query("query.fa", "results_after"))

CLI equivalent: kmhelpers design coli_update/ -o coli_db/ -n coli -S update, then kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/update/coli.yaml -o coli_build/

RESULT

The new sample scores 1.0 on its own contig, and GCA_000780515 still scores 1.0 on query.fa. coli_g0 now holds 6 samples.

docs.title: Python API (advanced)
docs.text: This page extends the Python API tutorial without changing kmhelpers: the pipeline steps exchange plain files (JSONL sample list, profile.yaml, layout and index definitions, build scripts), so any step can be replaced, fed with your own data or post-processed. The snippets run in the tutorial's working directory, next to coli_dataset/, coli_db/ and coli_build/, and reuse its reset_index_registry() and build() functions.

docs.title: Bypass the automatic listing
docs.text: SampleLister scanning a directory names each sample after its file and counts its k-mers. To control names, grouping, locations or counts, give it a sample list, or write its JSONL output yourself. See When to use a sample list.

docs.title: Generate a sample list from metadata
docs.text:
Name samples after a metadata table instead of their file names:

import os

from pykmhelpers.pipeline.sample_lister import SampleLister

strains = {
    "GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1": "strain_A",
    "GCA_001076125.1_ASM107612v1": "strain_B",
    "GCA_001417575.1_ASM141757v1": "strain_C",
}
with open("strains.txt", "w") as f:
    for accession, strain in strains.items():
        f.write(f"{strain} coli_dataset/{accession}_genomic.fna.gz\n")

os.makedirs("strains_db/list", exist_ok=True)
SampleLister(
    output_file="strains_db/list/strains.jsonl",
    input_list="strains.txt",
    kmer_size=25,
    do_grouping=False,
).run()
RESULT 
{"name": "strain_A", "files": ["coli_dataset/GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1_genomic.fna.gz"], "kmer_count": 10898876}

Each line is [sample_id] file_1[,file_2,...] [kmer_count]: list several comma-separated files to group them into one sample, and add a count to skip ntcard. Relative paths are resolved from the directory of the list file. See Input formats.

docs.title: Write the JSONL yourself
docs.text:
The JSONL file is the contract between list and the next steps: a header line with the k-mer size, then one {"name", "files", "kmer_count"} object per sample. Writing it directly skips SampleLister, for example to reuse k-mer counts computed by another tool or an earlier run:

import json

with open("coli_db/list/coli_samples_initial.jsonl") as f:
    counted = [json.loads(line) for line in f][1:]

os.makedirs("reuse_db/list", exist_ok=True)
with open("reuse_db/list/reuse.jsonl", "w") as f:
    f.write(json.dumps({"k": 25, "assembled": True, "abundance_min": 1}) + "\n")
    for s in counted:
        path = os.path.abspath(os.path.join("coli_dataset", s["files"][0]))
        entry = {"name": s["name"], "files": [path], "kmer_count": s["kmer_count"]}
        f.write(json.dumps(entry) + "\n")
INFO
  • k is required in the header; assembled and abundance_min are written by list and kept for consistency.
  • Use absolute file paths when the JSONL is not written by list.
  • kmer_count must be positive: it sizes the Bloom filter of the sample. For raw reads, count solid k-mers (seen at least twice), as list does with is_assembled=False.

docs.title: Filter samples between steps
docs.text:
Load the JSONL, keep or rename samples, write it back, then continue with SpanProfiler and IndexComposer. Here, small assemblies are left out:

from pykmhelpers.pipeline.composer import IndexComposer
from pykmhelpers.pipeline.span_profiler import SpanProfiler

with open("reuse_db/list/reuse.jsonl") as f:
    header, *samples = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

kept = [s for s in samples if s["kmer_count"] >= 5_000_000]
with open("reuse_db/list/reuse.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for entry in [header, *kept]:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry) + "\n")

SpanProfiler(
    input_file="reuse_db/list/reuse.jsonl",
    output_dir="reuse_db/profile",
    n_groups=2,
    base=1.1,
).run()
reset_index_registry()
IndexComposer(profiles_file="reuse_db/profile/profile.yaml", name="reuse").run(
    input_file="reuse_db/list/reuse.jsonl",
    output_dir="reuse_db/compose",
    run_id="initial",
)
RESULT

7 of the 10 samples are kept, and reuse_db/compose/reuse/initial/reuse.yaml is ready to build.

The same applies to the other files: profile.yaml (see profile) and the index definitions (see compose) are plain YAML that can be reviewed or edited before the next step.

docs.title: Run the build outside Python
docs.text:
ApplyMode.PLAN generates the commands without running them, and write_script() saves them as bash scripts. Plan from Python, then run the build where and when you want: another machine with the same paths, a job scheduler, or after review.

from pykmhelpers.pipeline.index_ops import ApplyMode, IndexOps, IndexOpsConfig

reset_index_registry()
ops = IndexOps(IndexOpsConfig(workdir="reuse_build", kmindex_threads=4))
result = ops.run("reuse_db/compose/reuse/initial/reuse.yaml", mode=ApplyMode.PLAN)
ops.write_script()
print(result.status)

ls reuse_build/assets/initial/
# kmhelpers_apply.sh  reuse_g0_initial.sh  reuse_g0_initial_merge.sh  ...
bash reuse_build/assets/initial/kmhelpers_apply.sh
INFO

There is one <part>.sh script per group of parts (the kmindex builds), one <part>_merge.sh (publication into the registry and cleanup), and kmhelpers_apply.sh running them all in order. Each script stops at the first failing command. See plan.

docs.title: Stream query results
docs.text:
QueryRunnerConfig(on_result=...) calls a function with the results of each query file as soon as it completes, without waiting for the other files or reading the output files. Results come as one KmindexQueryResult per sub-index, with items as {index: {query: {sample: score}}}:

from pykmhelpers import QueryRunner, QueryRunnerConfig

best = {}


def keep_best(results):
    """Keep the best sample of each query sequence, over all sub-indexes."""
    for result in results:
        for queries in result.items.values():
            for query, samples in queries.items():
                for sample, score in samples.items():
                    if score > best.get(query, ("", 0.0))[1]:
                        best[query] = (sample, score)


QueryRunner(
    QueryRunnerConfig(
        registry_path="coli_build",
        output_dir="results_stream",
        output_format=None,  # keep only the raw kmindex output
        on_result=keep_best,
    )
).run(["query.fa", "query_update.fa"])
print(best)
RESULT 
{'JSPL01000060.1': ('GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1_genomic', 1.0),
 'U00096.3': ('GCA_000005845_2_ASM584v2_genomic', 1.0)}

docs.title: Merge and summarize results
docs.text:
The CLI merges the sub-indexes by loading every raw output file of a query into one KmindexQueryResult. Do the same to use its statistics and formats:

import glob

from pykmhelpers import KmindexQueryResult

merged = KmindexQueryResult()
for path in glob.glob("results_stream/query_update/kmindex_output/*.jsonl"):
    merged.load_jsonl(path)

merged.match_stats(threshold=0.5)   # one row per query sequence
merged.sample_stats(threshold=0.8)  # one row per matched sample
merged.convert("json", threshold=0.8)  # also "tsv", "yaml"
RESULT

sample_stats(threshold=0.8) keeps 2 samples: GCA_000005845 (1.0) and GCA_000938575 (0.87), a close relative of the K-12 reference.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text: The classes, parameters and files used on this page are the public interface. Methods starting with _ are internal and may change between versions; if a customization needs one, please open an issue.

docs.title: Step-by-step: list → profile → compose → plan → apply
docs.text: This page is a companion to the E. coli tutorial. It assumes you have already followed the main steps and are looking for a deeper understanding of what each sub-command does, or want to run stages individually to inspect or re-run a specific part of the pipeline.

docs.title: design
docs.text: The three steps below are equivalent to Step 2 of the tutorial.

docs.title: Step 2.1 - Scan samples and count k-mers (list)
docs.text:
mkdir -p coli_db/list
kmhelpers list coli_dataset/ -o coli_db/list/coli.jsonl -k 25
I/O

Input: coli_dataset/ Output: coli_db/list/coli.jsonl

INFO

list scans coli_dataset/ for sequence files, counts k-mers with ntcard (k = 25), and writes one JSONL record per file (sample) to coli_db/list/coli.jsonl.

Why scan a directory rather than pass a sample list?

A directory scan names each sample after its file and counts its k-mers. A sample list lets you set names, reuse k-mer counts, group files freely and mix locations - see When to use a sample list.

RESULT

The header line records the shared parameters; every subsequent line is one sample:

{"description": "Generated by kmhelpers list", "date": "2026-06-29T12:58:33.254120", "root_path": "/path/to/coli_dataset", "k": 25, "assembled": true, "abundance_min": 1}
{"name": "GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1_genomic", "files": ["GCA_000780515.1_ASM78051v1_genomic.fna.gz"], "kmer_count": 10898876}
{"name": "GCA_001076125_1_ASM107612v1_genomic", "files": ["GCA_001076125.1_ASM107612v1_genomic.fna.gz"], "kmer_count": 10180102}
...

docs.title: Step 2.2 - Profile the k-mer distribution (profile)
docs.text:
kmhelpers profile coli_db/list/coli.jsonl -o coli_db/profile/ -b 1.1 -g 2
I/O

Input: coli_db/list/coli.jsonl Output: coli_db/profile/profile.yaml, coli_db/profile/groups.png

INFO

A span is an integer bucket that summarises a sample's k-mer count:

\[ s = \left\lfloor \log_{\text{base}}(n) \right\rfloor \]

where \(n\) is the sample's distinct k-mer count. All samples whose k-mer count falls in the same bucket \([\text{base}^s,\, \text{base}^{s+1})\) share span \(s\) and are indexed together in one sub-index.

The Bloom filter allocated for that sub-index is sized for the worst case of the bucket - the maximum k-mer count \(\text{base}^{s+1}\) - so every sample in the span fits:

\[ \text{bf_size} = \left\lceil \frac{f \cdot \text{base}^{s+1}}{8} \right\rceil \times 8 \qquad \text{where } f = \frac{-\ln p}{(\ln 2)^2} \]

\(p\) is the false-positive rate (default 0.25) and the \(\times 8\) rounding aligns the size to a byte boundary.

False-positive rate and findere

A higher \(p\) reduces Bloom-filter size and therefore disk footprint, at the cost of more false positives. At query time the findere algorithm compensates by querying \((k+z)\)-mers instead of \(k\)-mers, reducing the effective false-positive rate to \(p^z\):

\[ p_{\text{eff}} = p^z \]

Recommended settings: build with --fp 0.25 (default), query with -z 6 (default), giving \(0.25^6 \approx 0.024\,\%\) effective FP rate.

Lucas Robidou and Pierre Peterlongo. findere: fast and precise approximate membership query. SPIRE 2021, Springer, pp. 151–163. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-86692-1_13

Choosing base and the number of groups

base controls bucket width. With base=2.0 (default) each bucket spans a 2× range of k-mer counts, producing few coarse spans. -b 1.1 narrows each bucket to a 10 % range, giving finer resolution at the cost of more spans. -g 2 then requests that those spans be merged into 2 groups. For a dataset this small and uniform, -g 1 (a single group) would actually be the optimal choice; we use -g 2 here to illustrate how grouping works - pick a value that fits your own distribution.

RESULT

profile writes three output files to coli_profile/:

profile.yaml

Records global parameters and one named profile per grouping. The baseline profile preserves the natural 5-span distribution; 2_groups merges them into two sub-indices:

false_positive_rate: 0.25
span_base: 1.1
sample_count: 10
biggest_sample: ('GCA_000780515_1_ASM78051v1', 10898876)
max_kmer_count: 11971516
default_profile: 2_groups
profiles:
baseline:
    span_list: [161, 167, 168, 169, 170]
    bloom_size: [14649392, 25952288, 28547520, 31402272, 34542496]
    sample_dist: [5, 1, 2, 1, 1]
    disk_usage: [1.47e+07B, 2.6e+07B, 2.86e+07B, 3.14e+07B, 3.46e+07B]
    size_ratio: ['0.109', '0.192', '0.211', '0.232', '0.256']
    total_size: 1.35e+08B
    bytes_per_sample: 1.35e+07B
2_groups:
    span_list: [161, 170]
    bloom_size: [14649392, 34542496]
    sample_dist: [5, 5]
    disk_usage: [1.47e+07B, 3.46e+07B]
    size_ratio: ['0.298', '0.702']
    total_size: 4.92e+07B
    bytes_per_sample: 4.92e+06B
groups.png

A plot showing the k-mer count distribution, natural span boundaries, and the requested 2-group overlay.

Grouping affects both storage and query performance.

Storage

kmindex stores samples in packs of 8 (bit-packing), so a sub-index with 1 sample occupies the same disk space as one with 8. In the baseline profile, spans 167, 169 and 170 hold only 1–2 samples each - those near-empty packs waste most of their allocated space, bringing the total to 135 MB. In this case, merging the 5 sub-indices into 2 reduces the number of packs from 5 to 2 (one per group), cutting the total to 50 MB.

Query time

Each sub-index is composed of multiple partition files (kmindex terminology). Query performance on large datasets is dominated by disk latency rather than CPU, so every sub-index multiplies the number of partitions that must be opened and read. Fewer sub-indices means fewer partition files accessed per query, directly reducing that latency overhead.

docs.title: Step 2.3 - Compose index definitions (compose)
docs.text:
kmhelpers compose coli_db/list/coli.jsonl \
    -o coli_db/compose/ \
    -n coli \
    -S initial \
    -pf coli_db/profile/profile.yaml
I/O

Input: coli_db/list/coli.jsonl, coli_db/profile/profile.yaml Output: coli_db/compose/coli/initial/, with coli.yaml as the entry point

INFO

compose reads the sample list and the profile, then writes index definition files into coli_db/compose/coli/initial/. Pass the coli.yaml file in that directory to plan, build or apply in the next step. The sample-to-sub-index repartition is driven by the selected profile - here 2_groups, the default set by profile - whose Bloom-filter sizes are read from coli_db/profile/profile.yaml.

docs.title: build
docs.text: The two steps below are equivalent to Step 3 of the tutorial.

docs.title: Step 3.1 - Preview the build plan (plan)
docs.text:
kmhelpers plan coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/
I/O

Input: coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml Output: build scripts in coli_build/assets/ + validation report in coli_build/logs/

INFO

Before committing to a potentially long build, validate paths and preview the commands that will be executed: plan checks that every sample file exists, reports any missing paths, and prints the equivalent kmindex commands - without running them. Fix any path errors now rather than discovering them mid-build.

RESULT Validation report in coli_build/logs/
  • input_file -- path to the coli.yaml used as input
  • kmindex / kmhelpers -- tool versions detected at runtime
  • span -- one entry per sub-index: sample count and estimated disk size
  • run -- validation result (SUCCESS / FAILURE) per sub-index
Build scripts in coli_build/assets/
  • coli_g<span>_initial.sh -- one script per sub-index (coli_g0, coli_g1): one kmindex build call per part, with Bloom-filter size, k-mer size, and output paths pre-filled from the profile, then the merge into the sub-index and the deletion of the merged parts. Each script stops at the first failing command.
  • kmhelpers_apply.sh -- runs every sub-index script in order.

docs.title: Step 3.2 - Build the index (apply or bash)
docs.text:
applybash 
kmhelpers apply coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml -o coli_build/
I/O

Input: coli_db/compose/coli/initial/coli.yaml Output: coli_build/index.json + one folder per sub-index, coli_build/coli_g0/ and coli_build/coli_g1/ - ready-to-query index 

bash coli_build/assets/kmhelpers_apply.sh
I/O

Input: coli_build/assets/kmhelpers_apply.sh Output: coli_build/index.json + one folder per sub-index, coli_build/coli_g0/ and coli_build/coli_g1/ - ready-to-query index

RESULT

Once complete, the index is registered in coli_build/index.json and ready to query.

docs.title: Update an existing index: design → build
docs.text: This page is a companion to the E. coli tutorial. It shows how to add samples to an index that already exists, without rebuilding it from scratch. It assumes you have already followed the main steps and have coli_db/ and coli_build/ on disk.

docs.title: Step 1 - Download a new sample
docs.text:
Download it into its own directory, coli_update/: design scans the whole directory, and the samples already indexed must not be listed again.

mkdir -p coli_update && cd coli_update
wget "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/005/845/GCA_000005845.2_ASM584v2/GCA_000005845.2_ASM584v2_genomic.fna.gz"
cd ..
I/O

Input: one NCBI FTP URL (E. coli K-12 MG1655 reference assembly) Output: coli_update/GCA_000005845.2_ASM584v2_genomic.fna.gz

docs.title: Step 2 - Design the update session (design)
docs.text:
Re-run design with the same -o and -n as Step 2 of the tutorial, and a fresh -S session ID:

kmhelpers design coli_update/ -o coli_db/ -n coli -S update
I/O

Input: coli_update/, existing layout coli_db/compose/coli_layout.yaml Output: coli_db/compose/coli/update/coli.yaml

INFO

design detects the existing layout file at coli_db/compose/coli_layout.yaml, skips the profile step, and composes only the new samples. The k-mer size, span base and grouping of the initial run are reused, so the new sub-indices stay compatible with the existing ones.

docs.title: Step 3 - Build the update session (build)
docs.text:
Build into the same BUILD_DIR as Step 3 of the tutorial:

kmhelpers build coli_db/compose/coli/update/coli.yaml -o coli_build/ --show-progress
I/O

Input: coli_db/compose/coli/update/coli.yaml Output: updated coli_g0 in coli_build/coli_g0/, updated coli_build/index.json

INFO

Each index keeps its folder, coli_build/<name>/. While the session is built, its runs and merges live in coli_build/work/update/, deleted at the end. Building the same session again resumes it, or does nothing if it finished.

Building a session into a BUILD_DIR that already holds the index triggers a merge. kmindex cannot add samples to an existing index in place, so the update merges the old and the new samples into a new index, which replaces the previous one in coli_build/coli_g0/: it now holds its initial samples plus the new one. The previous version is deleted once the new one is checked (--keep-previous keeps it in coli_build/work/update/previous/).

GCA_000005845 falls in the span bucket of coli_g0, so only that sub-index is merged. coli_g1 is untouched.

Disk space

The previous version and the updated one coexist on disk during the merge. Plan for at least twice the size of the sub-indices being updated.

docs.title: Step 4 - Query the updated index (query)
docs.text:
kmhelpers query -r coli_build/ -o results_update/ query.fa
RESULT

coli_g0 now holds 6 samples, the 5 initial ones plus GCA_000005845. query.fa comes from GCA_000780515, indexed in coli_g1, which still scores 1.0.

The previous version was deleted once the updated one was registered and checked. To compare both versions, build with --keep-previous: the previous coli_g0 is then left in coli_build/work/update/previous/coli_g0/, to delete once done.

docs.title: Step 5 - Check the result
docs.text:
# Registered indices and the samples they hold
kmhelpers manage -r coli_build/ list
kmhelpers manage -r coli_build/ info -n coli_g0
kmhelpers manage -r coli_build/ check
